sentences.t: Erton Köhler and the Adventist Authority Machine: Spiritual Integrity in Pieces Between Andrews University, Adventus, and Montemorelos

Behind the celebration of a Doctor of Ministry earned by the world president of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, Erton Köhler, a fundamental question remains: what happens to the moral authority of a religious institution when its own mechanisms of prestige escape critical scrutiny?
There are ceremonies that celebrate a journey.
And there are ceremonies that reveal a system.
The awarding of a Doctor of Ministry (D.Min.)
to Erton Köhler, president of the General Conference of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, belongs to the second category.
The image is powerful: a religious leader in academic regalia, a denominational university highly regarded within the community — Andrews University — an official ceremony, a doctoral title.
Everything seems to convey an obvious message: recognition, competence, legitimacy.

But in an organization that claims a worldwide spiritual mission, one question should always precede the celebration: Does what reinforces the image of authority necessarily reinforce moral and spiritual authority as well?
The case of Erton Köhler exposes this tension.
The Adventist world president obtained a Doctor of Ministry from Andrews University, an American Adventist academic institution.
The academic clarification is essential: a Doctor of Ministry is not a PhD (an academic research doctorate).
This distinction is not an administrative detail.
It touches directly on how an institution builds and presents its authority.
The D.Min.
is a professional doctorate aimed mainly at religious leaders and pastoral ministry practitioners.
It seeks to deepen pastoral practice, church leadership, and applied reflection.
The PhD corresponds to a research doctorate based on producing an original scholarly contribution.
In the academic world, this distinction is clear, since it does not open the same rights.
But in the public sphere, academic nuances often disappear behind the symbolic weight of the word „doctor.”
Because in a religious institution, a university title is never just a qualification.
It becomes a mark of credibility.
It can become an indicator of spiritual expertise.
And sometimes it becomes an instrument of authority.
For precisely this reason, transparency is not an option.
It is a moral requirement.
When the title becomes an instrument of power.
In modern societies, university degrees attest to a path taken, a formation, and intellectual work.
But in religious institutions they take on an additional dimension.
A religious official who holds a doctorate is not perceived merely as someone who has studied more.
He may be regarded as someone whose voice carries superior authority.
Herein lies the real stake.
Because spiritual authority is not conferred by a diploma.
It is not measured solely by academic titles.
It is built through coherence between the principles proclaimed and the practices observed.
An institution that teaches its members integrity must hold an even higher standard for its own leaders.
The problem, then, is not simply the diploma obtained.
The problem is what that diploma represents within a system of religious power.
The Adventist paradox: proclaiming truth while tolerating one’s own untruths.
The Seventh-day Adventist Church was historically built around several core values: education, moral rigor, the pursuit of truth, and the training of leaders.
But this foundation comes with a responsibility.
The more educational institutions an organization holds, the more exemplary its governance of them must be.
Yet, like other human institutions, the Adventist world is not immune to the tensions of power: protecting its image, the weight of hierarchy, the difficulty of acknowledging dysfunction.
The Romanian precedent: Adventus Cernica, the University of Montemorelos, and the question of institutional responsibility.

The controversies surrounding Adventus University in Romania — which I documented in Edupedu (https://www.edupedu.ro/scandalul-diplomelor-cazul-universitatilor-religioase-si-intrebarile-deschise-despre-integritatea-academica/) — formerly the Adventist Theological Institute of Cernica — and the case of the questionable doctoral diplomas issued by Montemorelos Adventist University in Mexico, a case I also documented at the same link, raised significant questions about academic integrity within the Adventist confessional environment.

For example, regarding diplomas awarded by Adventus to cohorts of pastors who had not completed full undergraduate studies, I showed how, in the 1990s, police and prosecutors conducted detailed investigations into the training, academic records, credential equivalencies, and validation mechanisms involved.

The judicial proceedings did not end in criminal convictions because the statute of limitations had run out on the facts examined, but their effects remain intact — diplomas produce effects, so administrative review remains possible at any time, and revocation of diplomas is always possible.
A religious institution cannot limit its analysis solely to the legal framework, because faith raises the question: „What should an institution that claims to defend truth have done?”
Even if a statute of limitations can block a conviction, it does not block an institution from historical, moral, and institutional reflection.
The problem is not the error.
It is the absence of institutional courage.
The essential question is not whether errors exist, but how they are handled.
A solid church must be able to acknowledge its mistakes and say: „Here is what happened.
Here is what was problematic.
Here is what was corrected.
Here are the safeguards put in place to prevent it from happening again.”
When protecting the image becomes the priority, the crisis deepens.
Because a church does not live by its doctrines alone, but above all by people’s trust.
The Köhler case, then, goes far beyond the matter of a single diploma.

It reveals a deeper question about the concentration of multiple forms of authority: spiritual authority, administrative authority, academic authority, control over an educational network, and considerable institutional communication power.
These forms of power are not automatically equivalent.
A high position within a religious hierarchy does not guarantee moral superiority.
A university degree does not guarantee spiritual wisdom.
An institutional office does not guarantee ethical exemplarity.
The more concentrated power becomes, the stronger the mechanisms of oversight must be.
The history of religious institutions shows a constant: the gravest crises rarely arise when there is too much control — as with the Inquisition and all systems of concentrated clerical power.
They arise when loyalty to the institution becomes more important than truth toward the institution.
The question Adventism must confront.
Erton Köhler is not merely an individual in this reflection.
He becomes the revealer of a deeper question: can a worldwide church continue to claim superior moral authority if it refuses to apply to itself the standards it demands of others?
The answer will not come from a university ceremony.
It will not come from a new title.
It will come from an institution’s capacity to accept critical scrutiny, transparency, and being called into question.
But, as in Romania, the church’s leadership is evidently weak — very weak — and not equal to the mission it holds.

We have seen this too in the most recent case involving sexual abuse allegations within the church in Romania, which can be read about here (https://recorder.ro/doctrina-tacerii-pentru-influenta-politica-si-bani-publici-biserica-adventista-tolereaza-in-mijlocul-ei-un-barbat-acuzat-de-abuz-sexual-de-mai-multe-femei/), as well as in the case of the complete indifference regarding the protection of former communist secret police collaborators who now hold leadership positions in Romania, which greatly affects the credibility of the Romanian Adventist Church.

I have also written about this here (https://www.contributors.ro/evangheliile-lustratiei-religioase-postdecembriste-toleranta-ecumenica-la-vanzarea-lui-iuda/), and recent documents have been published on independent community digital platforms (Forumul comunitatilor — https://www.facebook.com/groups/1027181923640239/permalink/1027283780296720/).
A Church does not lose its authority because it is criticized; it loses it when it uses its authority to avoid criticism.
True spiritual integrity is not a diploma, is not an office, is not an institutional distinction — it is an organization’s capacity to choose truth, even when that truth is uncomfortable.
Even deeply so.
